Leach's storm-petrel (Oceanodroma leucorhoa) is a small, long-lived seabird that exhibits a remarkably slow pace of life, typical of many pelagic Procellariiformes. Field studies on Kent Island, New Brunswick, have provided detailed demographic data for this species. For eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 41 days [ab = approximately 41 days], a duration consistent with the extended embryonic development seen in other hydrobatids that nest in cool, humid burrows. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling emerges with a wet weight at birth of 8.5 grams [Wwb = 8.5 grams], a modest mass representing only a small fraction of the adult body size. This initial mass is supported by substantial yolk reserves, and the chick is brooded continuously by both parents for the first several days of life, relying on a diet of regurgitated oil and partially digested prey items.

During the nestling period, the chick undergoes a remarkable transformation, accumulating mass at a rapid rate until it approaches its asymptotic size. The ultimate wet weight, or the asymptotic body mass for the nestling, has been recorded at 87 grams [Wwi = 87 grams], a value that closely approximates the average adult mass for the species. Under the thermal conditions typical of an active, homeothermic nestling, which correspond to a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the time since birth at fledging is approximately 70 days [tx = approximately 70 days]. Fledging marks the completion of the nest-dependent phase, after which the young bird departs the burrow and begins an independent existence at sea. This extended nestling period is energetically costly for the provisioning adults, who must commute long distances to forage for the growing chick.

The onset of reproductive capability occurs relatively late in this species, contributing to its slow life-history strategy. Reaching puberty, defined as the attainment of full gonadal maturity, requires a protracted developmental period. Field evidence indicates that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 210 days [tp = approximately 210 days] when assessed at the species' active metabolic temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. However, despite achieving physiological maturity at this age, first-year birds rarely breed; they often spend additional years at sea refining foraging skills and establishing pairing bonds. Consequently, the actual age at which a bird first participates in a breeding colony is substantially later than the onset of puberty, a separation that is common among long-lived seabirds where deferred reproduction enhances lifetime fitness.

The age at first successful reproduction is a key demographic parameter for this species, marking the initiation of an individual's reproductive contribution to the population. Longitudinal banding studies have revealed that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 5 years [tR = approximately 5 years], measured at the species' characteristic body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding is typical of small procellariiforms, which invest heavily in a single egg per nesting attempt. Once a bird begins breeding, it exhibits high annual adult survival, a necessary counterbalance to low annual fecundity. The maximum reproductive output of this species reaches one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch] and one brood annually [F_R_i = one brood annually], reflecting the constrained breeding schedule typical of this pelagic seabird.

The overall lifespan of Leach's storm-petrel reflects its position at the slow end of the life-history continuum. Maximum recorded longevity, based on recaptures of banded individuals, is 36 years [am = 36 years], a figure far exceeding what would be predicted for a bird of its 87-gram adult mass at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This survival rate is evaluated within the context of the species' active metabolic body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a thermal regime consistent across many seabird species. Such an extended lifespan, coupled with the deferred onset of breeding and the production of a single offspring annually, defines a life-history strategy heavily reliant on high adult survival to offset low and infrequent reproductive success. This strategy is an adaptation to the unpredictable marine environment, ensuring that adults have multiple opportunities to reproduce over a long lifetime.
